#### Recomputing after a rule change

`final_mark` and its siblings are STORED computes. Odoo recomputes a stored
compute when one of its dependencies moves - not when the method that produces
it is edited. So a rule change leaves every row already on disk holding the
number the old rule gave it, and those rows are not stable: they flip one at a
time the next time a rescore or a threshold edit happens to touch a dependency.

`tools/backfill_final_marks.py` forces that recompute through
`_recompute_question_marks`, and prints which attempts changed verdict together
with their release state, so a run that moves an already-released result says so
rather than doing it quietly.

**It recomputes; it does not re-grade.** Two answer types need the grader to look
again rather than arithmetic:

- an `image_label` answer scored before the per-box contract has no per-box raws
  on disk to re-aggregate from, and
- an `image_ab` answer's stored `llm_raw_100` is the OLD blended figure rather
  than the justification alone.

For those, run `action_regrade_for_component_scoring` on the affected
assessments first, let the scoring cron drain, and only then run the backfill.
Running the backfill alone leaves those two types recomputed from stale inputs.
Unlike every other queueing path, `action_regrade_for_component_scoring` has no
stopping, cancelled-paper or erased-attempt guard, so run it only on papers you
have checked by hand.


## 4.7 Scoring, for stakeholders

Was `docs/ETP_KNOWLEDGE_BASE.md (4.7 Scoring, for stakeholders)`. The same rules in plain language, with worked examples and known limitations.

A plain-language guide. No code required.

This is the stakeholder version of section 4.6. Same rules, written for someone
who has never opened the module.

---

### The one-paragraph version

A question is **not** worth 1 mark. It is worth 1 mark **for each part it is made
of**, and a candidate wins or loses each part on its own. A multiple-choice
question with three sub-questions is worth 3 marks, and getting two of them right
earns 2. A candidate's score is the marks they earned over the marks the paper
was worth, and they pass if that percentage reaches the assessment's pass
threshold (70% by default). Alongside that, the system records a second, more detailed
number called the **raw score**, which measures *how close* they came on each
part, out of the same total. The raw score is for reviewers only. It never
decides anything.

> **What changed.** Scoring used to be all-or-nothing per question: one wrong
> sub-question, or one weak write-up, cost the entire question. It is now
> part-by-part. Marks totals are therefore **larger numbers than before** (a
> 10-question paper might be out of 31, not out of 10) and mid-range candidates
> generally score higher, because credit that used to be thrown away is now kept.

> **What the 19.0.3.23.0 release changed.** Not the marking rules, with one
> exception: the 55-point cap no longer applies to Image Prompt and Video Prompt
> answers (section 6). It changed the AI grader's instructions
> (shorter, text only, reasons written for the candidate), added a re-score for
> one answer, made Kill and Release safe to press while grading is running, and
> lets a candidate see the grader's one-line verdict on a released answer. The
> first paper graded under the new instructions is held until an admin has
> spot-checked about 10 answers (see section 10).

---

### 1. "Normal" and "Raw" are not two modes

This is the most common misunderstanding, so it goes first.

There is **no setting** that switches an assessment between "normal scoring" and
"raw scoring". Both numbers are calculated at the same time, from the same
inputs. They just apply different rules, and **they do not cover the same things**.

| | The mark (the "normal" score) | The raw score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What it looks like** | A whole number of marks, e.g. 8 out of 11. Never a fraction. | A decimal, e.g. 8.21 out of 11. |
| **The question it answers** | *Which parts cleared the bar?* | *By how much, on each part?* |
| **What it covers** | **Every** part of the paper. | **Every** part of the paper - the same ones, out of the same total. |
| **Does it decide pass or fail?** | **Yes. Always.** | **No. Never.** |
| **Does the candidate see it?** | Yes, as marks, e.g. "8 / 11" | No. Admin and reviewer only. |

**How to read them together:** the mark tells you who cleared the bar. The raw
tells you by how much. A candidate can clear every bar and still show a raw well
under 100%. Read the raw *beside* the mark, never instead of it.

> **Why both exist.** With marks alone, an essay graded 69 and an essay graded 4
> both read 0 against a threshold of 70, and you cannot tell them apart. The raw
> score preserves that difference for a human reviewer.

**The two percentages share a denominator.** Both divide by every mark on the
paper. What differs is the top of the fraction: the score counts parts that
cleared the bar, the raw counts how close each came. They will usually not match
- the raw is normally the higher of the two - and that gap is the partial credit
the marks round away. See section 8.

---

### 2. The rules that apply to every question

**Every *part* of a question is worth exactly 1 mark.** There are no per-question
weights and no per-part weights. A hard part and an easy part are worth the same.
Nothing is weighted against anything else.

There are exactly three kinds of part:

1. **A sub-question with a marked correct answer.** One mark each. This covers
   every multiple-choice pick, on any question type, including each comparison
   axis of an Image A/B question.
2. **An AI-graded written answer.** One mark, on Rubric, Image Prompt, Video
   Prompt and Image A/B questions. (An Image A/B question authored without an
   official reasoning has no written part: there is nothing to grade it
   against.)
3. **A set of labelling boxes, taken as a whole.** One mark, on an Image
   Labelling question, however many boxes it has.

**A part is won or lost on its own.** There is no half a mark inside a part, and
no rule where failing one part cancels another. Getting two of three
sub-questions right earns 2 marks, not 0.

**The denominator is the length of the paper, not the questions that were
answered.** If a paper is worth 31 marks, a candidate who answers half of it
still scores out of 31, not out of what they attempted.

> This was once a live bug. An 8-question paper was being scored out of 3, so
> answering the three easy questions and abandoning the rest read **100%, PASS**.
> The fix was to make the paper's full worth the denominator, full stop.

**Two settings, two jobs.** The assessment's **Subjective Pass Threshold**
(default **70**) is used as:

1. The **bar each AI-graded written answer must clear** to earn its mark.
2. The **bar each individual labelling box must clear**, and then the bar the
   share of cleared boxes must itself clear.

The assessment's **Pass Threshold** is the **overall pass mark** for the whole
attempt. A new assessment starts at the Settings default (**70** unless an admin
changes it). An assessment made before this setting existed has none set, and
uses its Subjective Pass Threshold instead, exactly as it always did.

**There are no sections, categories or modules.** Marks roll straight up into the
attempt total. There is no per-section score and no per-section weighting.

**There are no letter grades, bands or maturity levels.** The only three outcomes
are **Pending**, **Pass** and **Fail**.

**There are no conditional or "show if" questions.** Every candidate sees every
question on their paper. Nothing is hidden, so nothing drops out of the total.

**There is no "Not Applicable" answer.** In an Image A/B question, "Both Good" and
"Both Bad" look like N/A but they are ordinary answer options - one of them can be
the correct answer, and picking it is scored like any other choice.

---

### 3. The question types

There are **seven**.

| Type | What the candidate does | What it is worth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Objective - MCQ** | Picks one option per sub-question. | 1 mark per sub-question. |
| **Objective - MSQ** | Picks several options per sub-question. | 1 mark per sub-question. |
| **Subjective - Rubric** | Writes an answer in prose. Graded by AI. | 1 mark for the writing, plus 1 for any multiple-choice sub-question it carries. |
| **Image - A/B Evaluation** | Compares two images across several axes, then explains the call. | 1 mark per comparison axis, plus 1 for the explanation when the question has an official reasoning. |
| **Image - Prompt** | Writes an image-generation prompt. Graded by AI. | 1 mark for the prompt, plus 1 per multiple-choice check. |
| **Image - Labelling** | Labels numbered boxes on an image. Graded by AI. | 1 mark for the box set as a whole, plus 1 per multiple-choice check. |
| **Video - Prompt** | Writes a video-generation prompt. Graded by AI. | 1 mark for the prompt, plus 1 per multiple-choice check. |

An eighth type, a two-plate variant of Image Labelling, was retired. Existing
questions of that type were folded into ordinary Image Labelling.

They fall into three families:

- **Machine-marked against an answer key:** MCQ, MSQ
- **AI-graded against a rubric:** Rubric, Image Prompt, Video Prompt, Labelling
- **Both at once:** Image A/B, and any of the above carrying multiple-choice checks

---

### 4. How each type is scored

#### 4.1 MCQ - pick one

Each sub-question is worth 1 mark, earned when the candidate picked the correct
option and nothing else.

A single-sub-question MCQ is worth 1 mark, exactly as before. A three-sub-question
MCQ is worth 3, and getting two right earns 2. Under the old rule that same
candidate scored 0.

Multiple choice carries a raw too, and for it the raw simply **equals the mark**
- a sub-question is either exactly right or it is not, so there is no "by how
much" to record. It is included so that the raw and the mark describe the same
paper out of the same total; a paper of pure multiple choice therefore shows a
raw identical to its mark, rather than no raw at all.

---

#### 4.2 MSQ - pick several

Each sub-question is worth 1 mark. The candidate's set of ticks must match the
answer key **exactly**: one option missed, or one extra option ticked, and that
sub-question scores 0.

##### Worked example

One MSQ sub-question with 5 options, 3 of which are correct.

| What the candidate ticked | Mark |
| --- | --- |
| All 3 correct options, nothing else | **1** |
| 2 of the 3 correct options | 0 |
| All 3 correct options, plus 1 wrong one | 0 |
| All 5 options | 0 |
| 1 correct option | 0 |
| Nothing correct | 0 |

**Ticking everything scores 0.** That is deliberate. An older raw score gave
multiple choice partial credit with no penalty for wrong picks, so a candidate
who ticked every box read a perfect raw while earning nothing. That rule is gone:
a sub-question's raw is now simply its mark, so ticking everything reads 0 in
both columns.

Each sub-question stands alone, so on a three-part MSQ a candidate who is exact
on two parts and one option short on the third earns **2 of 3**.

---

#### 4.3 Rubric, Image Prompt, Video Prompt - AI graded

The candidate writes something. An AI grader reads it against the question's
rubric and returns a number from 0 to 100.

- **Mark:** 1 if that number is **at or above the threshold**, 0 if below.
- **Raw:** the grader's number, kept as a decimal (a graded 84 is a raw of 0.84).

##### Worked examples

Assessment threshold is 70.

| Grader's number | Raw | Mark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 92 | 0.92 | **1** |
| 71 | 0.71 | **1** |
| 70 | 0.70 | **1** (at the threshold counts as clearing it) |
| 68 | 0.68 | 0 |
| 12 | 0.12 | 0 |

If the question also carries multiple-choice checks, those are separate marks on
top, decided independently of the writing.

**The grader's number is not taken on trust.** The AI has to itemise every
deduction it makes, with a reason and a quoted piece of evidence. The system then
rebuilds the score itself from those deductions (100 minus everything deducted)
and uses its own figure, not the AI's headline number. If the AI says "95" but
only itemises deductions worth 40 points, the score is 60, not 95. A gap of more
than about 1.5 points between the two flags the answer for human review.

**What the AI is given.** Text only: the question's answer key (written from
the image or video) and the candidate's answer. It never sees the media itself,
and it is never shown anything about the candidate beyond the answer. Its
reasons are written in plain words, because the candidate reads them once the
result is released. It runs at a low, fixed randomness (temperature 0.2), so
grading the same answer twice can differ by a few points.

---

#### 4.4 Image Labelling

The whole box set is worth **1 mark**, however many boxes there are. But the
grader does not score the set: it scores **each box individually**, 0 to 100. The
platform then does the marking itself, in two steps.

1. **Each box is judged on its own** against the threshold. A box clears or it
   does not.
2. **The share of boxes that cleared** is then judged against the same threshold.
   That decides the single mark.

##### Worked example

A 20-box question, threshold 60.

| Boxes clearing 60 | Share | Share as a percentage | Mark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 18 of 20 | 0.90 | 90% | **1** |
| 12 of 20 | 0.60 | 60% | **1** (at the bar counts as clearing it) |
| 11 of 20 | 0.55 | 55% | 0 |

The **raw** for the question is separate: it is the average of the individual box
scores. If the 20 box scores add up to 1250, the average is 62.5 and the raw is
**0.625**.

Three rules protect the count:

- **A box the candidate never attempted scores 0**, whatever the AI said about it.
  Graders reward a plausible-looking blank surprisingly often.
- **A box the AI failed to score also counts as 0**, and is still counted in the
  denominator. Otherwise an AI that returned one box out of twenty would make a
  one-box answer look complete.
- **A box only counts as attempted if the candidate typed at least 2 non-space
  characters in it.** A single letter, or a space, counts as skipped. Without that
  floor a candidate pads boxes with junk to inflate their coverage.

> **Previously a known limitation, now fixed.** A candidate who labelled 6 of 10
> boxes was supposed to be ceilinged at 60, but in practice this only raised an
> advisory flag for a human and did not lower the score. That ceiling has been
> removed and replaced with something stricter and simpler: **an unattempted box
> simply scores 0**, and it counts. The gap is closed.

---

#### 4.5 Image A/B

This type used to be the complicated one. It is now the plainest.

The candidate does two things: they pick a verdict on each comparison axis (which
image is better on sharpness, on lighting, and so on, plus one **Overall**
choice), and they write a justification explaining their call.

**Each comparison axis is worth 1 mark**, marked exactly like any other
multiple-choice sub-question: right or wrong, on its own. **The justification is
worth 1 further mark**, graded and thresholded exactly like any other written
answer.

So a question with 4 axes plus a justification is worth **5 marks**. Nothing is
blended, nothing is weighted, and no part cancels another. A question authored
without an official reasoning is worth its axes alone (4): with no standard to
grade the explanation against, it is not marked.

##### What was removed

Three rules that used to govern this type are gone, and any older description of
them is wrong:

- **The 0.75 / 0.25 blend.** Verdict accuracy and justification quality were mixed
  into a single number before either was marked. It was applied twice over, and it
  meant that on any assessment with a threshold of 75 or below the justification
  could not affect the mark at all, while still appearing to be worth a quarter of
  the question.
- **The 60-point cap for a wrong Overall choice.** It punished a wrong Overall
  preference through a number that no longer exists. The Overall Choice axis is
  now simply one of the axes, and is marked wrong when it is wrong.
- **The all-or-nothing rule across the two halves.** One wrong verdict used to
  cost the entire question.

##### Worked examples

An Image A/B question with 4 comparison axes plus a justification. Threshold 70.
The question is worth **5 marks**.

| | What happened | Marks | Old rule would have given |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | All 4 verdicts right, justification graded 80 | **5 / 5** | 1 / 1 |
| **B** | All 4 verdicts right, justification graded 20 | **4 / 5** | 1 / 1 |
| **C** | 3 of 4 verdicts right, justification graded 90 | **4 / 5** | 0 / 1 |
| **D** | Overall choice wrong, other 3 right, justification graded 90 | **4 / 5** | 0 / 1 |
| **E** | All 4 verdicts right, justification box left empty | **4 / 5** | 1 / 1 |

Read row **C** against row **B**: a candidate who missed a comparison but wrote
well, and a candidate who called every comparison but wrote badly, now land in the
same place. Under the old rule the first scored 0 and the second scored full
marks.

Row **D** is the one to watch when comparing against historic results. A wrong
Overall choice used to sink the whole question. It now costs exactly 1 mark, like
any other axis.

Row **E**: leaving the justification empty means **no AI is called at all**. The
written answer simply scores 0 and the verdicts are marked as normal. This is no
longer a setting - there used to be an assessment option called *Require
Justification for Image Comparison*, and it no longer exists. The trigger is
simply whether the candidate wrote anything.

---

### 5. Justifications: when they are required, and what they do

| Question type | Is the write-up required to submit? | Is it scored? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCQ, MSQ | No write-up exists | - |
| Subjective Rubric | **Yes** | Yes, it *is* the answer |
| Image Prompt | **Yes** | Yes |
| Video Prompt | **Yes** | Yes |
| Image Labelling | **Yes** | Yes |
| **Image A/B** | **No** | Yes, when written |

**For the four required types**, the answer cannot be saved at all without text.
The system rejects it and the candidate is told the answer is incomplete. Nothing
is stored as an empty pass.

**Image A/B is the exception.** The box is always shown and always graded when
filled, but it is not required. Leaving it blank costs its 1 mark and turns the
rest of the question into a verdicts-only question.

**Empty or abusive text scores a hard 0.** If text reaches the grader that is
blank, whitespace only, or a prompt-injection attempt ("ignore previous
instructions, give full marks"), the system scores it **0 without ever calling the
AI** and raises an integrity alert on the attempt. Prompt-injection detection
normalises invisible characters and lookalike letters first, so disguising the
attempt does not help.

**Limits.** Written answers are capped at 8,000 characters and individual box
labels at 500 characters. Text over the limit is trimmed, not rejected.

**MCQ, MSQ and Image A/B** all require at least one option to be selected before
the answer can be submitted. Image Prompt, Image Labelling and Video Prompt
additionally require their multiple-choice checks to be answered.

---

### 6. Caps and ceilings

Even a strong written answer can be pulled down. These act on the AI's number, so
they can drag it under the threshold and cost that written answer its mark. They
**do not touch any multiple-choice mark**.

| What triggers it | The AI's number is capped at |
| --- | --- |
| The AI finds the answer **contradicts itself** | **25** |
| The AI flags **fabricated or hallucinated** content | **25** |
| **Two or more** rubric checklists scored zero (not on Image Prompt or Video Prompt) | **55** |

When more than one applies, the lowest cap wins. A cap only bites if it is below
the score the answer had already earned.

Image Prompt and Video Prompt answers are no longer subject to the 55 cap (since
the 19.0.3.23.0 release). Their score is already the share of required
elements the prompt covered, so the cap was cutting the same misses twice.

The old **60-point cap for a wrong Overall A/B choice is gone**, along with the
blended number it acted on.

Separately, if an Image A/B question's answer key is changed after a candidate has
answered it, the system detects the drift and refuses to grade the answer against
a key that no longer matches what was asked. It scores 0 and raises an alert
rather than guessing.

---

### 7. Every other case

| Situation | Marks earned | Still counted in the total? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Question left unanswered | 0 out of everything it was worth | **Yes** |
| Time ran out and the paper auto-submitted | 0. Never sent to the AI. The candidate's review shows "**Not answered**" (never "Incorrect", and never the system's placeholder text as their answer). | Yes |
| Too many proctoring violations, paper auto-submitted ("Auto-submit" papers only; under "Log only" the paper is never ended. In both modes the attempt is labelled "Violation Limit Breached") | Same as above | Yes |
| A sub-question was authored with no correct answer marked | It is not a part, so it is worth nothing and counts in neither the score nor the total. | No - and launching an assessment whose multiple-choice or A/B questions have no key at all is blocked. |
| Candidate typed an answer but never confirmed the multiple-choice part of the same question | Held as a draft. Text is preserved, question does not count as answered. | Yes |
| The AI grader hit an outage or error | **Nothing yet** | The whole attempt is held at **Pending**, never failed |
| The AI grader is busy or at a limit (rate limit, daily or per-candidate spend cap, database connections full) | **Nothing yet**. No retry is used up; it is tried again on the grader's next round, and admins see the reason. | The whole attempt is held at **Pending** |
| An admin pressed **Kill** before an answer was graded | **Nothing yet** | The whole attempt is held at **Pending** until someone runs the grading again |
| Any AI-graded answer is still in the queue | **Nothing yet** | The whole attempt is held at **Pending** |

**On the grader rows:** an infrastructure outage, a limit, or an admin's Kill is
not the candidate's failure. The attempt waits for the grading to run rather
than being finalised as a 0. Kill keeps every mark already given.

**On "Not answered" vs "Awaiting grading":** the two labels exist so a reader can
tell an abandoned question apart from one still in the queue.

---

### 8. Adding it all up

```
Marks earned  =  the sum of every part's mark (each 0 or 1)
Marks possible = the sum of every part on the paper the candidate was given
Score         =  marks earned / marks possible
Result        =  PASS if that percentage reaches the pass threshold, otherwise FAIL
                 (unless anything is still pending, which overrides both)

Raw earned    =  the sum of every part's raw (each 0 to 1)
Raw possible  =  the same total as Marks possible
Raw percent   =  raw earned / raw possible
```

The candidate sees their score as **marks**, e.g. "8 / 11". The percentage is
internal and is never shown to them as a score.

**The denominators are the same, and that is the point.** Both divide by every
part on the paper. Only the numerators differ: a part that cleared its bar
contributes 1 mark whatever its quality, while the raw records the quality
itself. So the raw is normally a little higher than the mark, and the gap is the
partial credit the marks round away.

The raw used to leave multiple choice out of both sides. That produced two
figures out of two different totals for one attempt - "8 / 11" beside
"1.40 / 2" - which read as an error rather than a distinction. A multiple-choice
part's raw is now simply its mark.

#### Worked example: a full attempt

A paper of 5 questions. Threshold 70.

| Q | Type | Parts | What happened | Marks | Raw |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | MCQ | 1 sub-question | Correct | 1 / 1 | 1.00 |
| 2 | MSQ | 3 sub-questions | Exact on 2, one option short on the third | 2 / 3 | 2.00 |
| 3 | Rubric | 1 written answer | Graded 84 | 1 / 1 | 0.84 |
| 4 | Image A/B | 4 axes + 1 justification | 3 axes right, justification graded 55 | 3 / 5 | 3.55 |
| 5 | Image Labelling | 1 box set (20 boxes) | 18 boxes cleared; average box score 82 | 1 / 1 | 0.82 |

- **Marks: 8 out of 11 = 72.7%. Result: PASS.**
- **Raw: 8.21 out of 11 = 74.6%**, over the same 11 parts.

Three things to read off this:

1. **The same attempt would have failed under the old rules.** Q2 would have
   scored 0 (one part short of perfect) and Q4 would have scored 0 (one verdict
   wrong), giving 3 out of 5 = 60%, a fail. The candidate has not changed; the
   marking has.
2. **The two totals are both 11, and the 0.21 between them is the whole story.**
   The written answer graded 84 and the justification graded 55 are what pull the
   raw off the marks; every multiple-choice part contributes the same number to
   both. The raw is still not "the score, more precisely" - it never decides
   anything - but it can now be read straight against the mark beside it.
3. **The marks total is larger than the question count.** 11, not 5. Anyone
   comparing this attempt against a pre-change one must compare the percentages,
   never the marks.

---

### 9. Nothing reaches the candidate until a person releases it

No score, verdict or mark is visible to a candidate until an admin explicitly
releases that attempt.

- There is **no automatic release**. No scheduled job releases anything.
- There is **no un-release** once done. Nothing in the system can put results back
  out of sight.
- Releasing one candidate does **not** release the cohort. Releasing a whole
  cohort is a separate, deliberate action.
- Every Release button **asks first**. The cohort-wide one in Odoo shows how
  many candidates are being released and how many still have written answers
  with the grader.
- A candidate whose answers are **being graded at that very moment is skipped**,
  not released, and the admin is told so. The next click, a minute later,
  releases them with final marks.

Until then the candidate sees "Awaiting results" and nothing else - not the score,
not the pass mark position, not per-question feedback.

After release the candidate sees their marks and, per question, their answer
and its label ("Correct", "Partly correct (2 of 3)", "Incorrect", "Passed",
"Failed", "Not answered"). On an AI-graded answer they also see the grader's
feedback, the itemised deductions and credit, and the grader's one-line verdict
("The judge's verdict"). The verdict is shown only when it was written under the
grading instructions in use today: verdicts written earlier were addressed to
admins and are withheld. That rule is a switch, and it is on.

**Changing a mark after release.** An admin can re-score one answer, or chosen
answers of one candidate, after release, but only by confirming it on purpose:
it costs another AI call and can move a mark the candidate is looking at. The
old mark stays until the new grade succeeds.

---

### 10. Known limitations

Stated plainly, because they matter when interpreting results.

**1. The raw score is still not a grade.** It now covers the whole paper out of
the same total as the mark, which makes it much easier to read - and that is
exactly the risk. It is not a more precise version of the score and must never be
used on its own to rank candidates or feed an automated decision: it ignores
every pass threshold, so a candidate who missed the bar on every written answer
can still show a healthy raw. If ranking on it ever becomes the plan, this is the
first assumption to revisit.

**2. Historic results are not comparable mark for mark.** An attempt scored under
the old rules carries a smaller total out of a smaller denominator, and the same
performance generally earns a higher percentage now. Compare percentages, never
marks, and treat any trend line that crosses the change date with suspicion.

**3. The new grading instructions are checked on made-up answers only.** The
19.0.3.23.0 instructions were compared with the old ones on about 100 made-up
answers to real questions. They scored correct and wrong answers the same, and
were stricter on answers that address the grader. On one partial Image Prompt
answer they gave 0 where the old ones gave 40. So the first paper graded under
them is not released until an admin has spot-checked about 10 answers, partial
Image and Video Prompt answers included. Details: `ETP_PLANS_AND_STRATEGY.md`
§0.1.

**4. Nobody can type in a different AI mark.** A reviewer who disagrees can
re-score the answer, which runs the same grader again, but cannot overwrite the
mark by hand.

#### Previously listed here, now fixed

- **The review screen disagreeing with the marks.** A multiple-choice question
  with several sub-questions used to read "Incorrect" unless every sub-question
  was right. It now reads "Partly correct (2 of 3)", matching the marks. A
  question the clock took away reads "Not answered", not "Incorrect".
- **Video Prompt multiple-choice checks not required.** They are now required
  before the answer can be submitted, like Image Prompt and Image Labelling.

- **Multiple-choice picks that were collected but not scored.** Image Prompt,
  Image Labelling and Video Prompt questions can carry multiple-choice checks.
  Candidates were required to answer them, but the answers contributed nothing to
  any score. **They are now marked like any other sub-question**, one mark each.
  Expect these questions to be worth more marks than they used to be, and expect a
  candidate who answered those checks carelessly to score lower than the same
  attempt would have scored before.
- **The advisory-only labelling coverage ceiling.** A candidate who labelled 6 of
  10 boxes should have been ceilinged at 60 but only raised a review flag.
  **Unattempted boxes now simply score 0** and still count, which is stricter and
  needs no ceiling.
- **The Image A/B weights being applied twice.** The 0.75 / 0.25 split happened
  once inside the grader and again when the question's raw was composed, giving an
  effective 93.75 / 6.25. **The weights are gone entirely**, so the problem cannot
  arise.

---

### What the backend addon does

`assessments_be_v2` was, at the time of writing, a JSON API over the existing
`etp_assessment_pro` module. It did not reimplement business logic — it called the module's
own `action_*` methods, so Odoo and the Flutter app could not drift apart in behaviour.

- **Auth** — bearer tokens via `api_auth_gateway`, adopted for `auth="user"` routes in an
  `ir.http` override.
- **Authorisation** — Odoo groups (`require_manager` / `require_staff`) plus
  `record_read_guard`, which enforces the caller's own record rules. Per record, not per path.
- **Serialisers** that structurally cannot express an answer key in a candidate payload — the
  correct-answer field is absent from the shape rather than stripped conditionally.
- **CORS** with credentials, echoing one specific origin and never a wildcard.

The changes inside `etp_assessment_pro` itself are fixes, not features. Each is listed under
Defects.

### What the Flutter app does

The full operator console plus the candidate exam runner — dashboard, assessments,
generators, review queue, question bank, tags, responses, scoring, LLM budget, spend ledger,
settings and docs, with the runner covering all 7 question types.

#### Built in this cycle

- **Question editing.** Drafts and bank questions can now be edited, including the answer
  key. Previously it was approve-or-deny only, so a generated question with a typo cost
  another paid generation. Guards refuse a key naming an option that does not exist, a
  question with nothing correct, and a single-answer question with two correct options — and
  an option a candidate has already chosen cannot be deleted.
- **Scoring screen.** The grading pipeline had no UI at all; the only way to see whether the
  grader was running was to open Odoo.
- **Generator screen rebuilt** to match the Odoo form — question types as a dropdown with
  removable chips, Select all, Extra instructions, Sample questions and Reference files
  uploads, Advanced options collapsed.
- **Chatter.** One verb (Log note), Enter to log, newest at the bottom, search, emoji, file
  attachments (which needed new server support), full screen, and Emails moved to its own tab.
- **Navigation.** Analytics renamed Dashboard and made the landing screen; Start here renamed
  Docs and moved above Settings; spend ledger off the rail and cross-linked with LLM budget;
  ledger rows now open in full.
- Generator archive and restore, similarity ranking, question-count control, per-candidate
  release.

---

### Defects found and fixed

Every one of these was live. They are listed in full because the pattern matters more than
any individual bug: **most of them failed silently** — producing a wrong result with no error
recorded anywhere.

Evidence markers: **live** = reproduced against a running system · **unit** = proven by test
· **traced** = code path read, not reproduced.

#### Would have been visible to a customer

| Defect | Effect | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Answer key leaked mid-exam** | `/exam/<token>/review` built its rows with the post-release serialiser, which for mcq/msq emits the names of the correct options plus a live Correct/Incorrect verdict — to a candidate who had not submitted. | live |
| **Per-candidate release published the whole cohort** | The Release button on one attempt sent no evaluator ids, and the route treats an empty list as "release everyone". | live |
| **Candidate told "submitted" when nothing was** | One refused answer aborted the re-send loop before the submit call, leaving the attempt in progress on the server while the candidate walked away. | traced |
| **Exam link on every admin list row** | `access_token` is a bearer credential — whoever holds it can sit that person's paper. It was on every row of every list any Evaluator could fetch. | live |
| **No countdown for a resuming candidate** | The deadline was computed before the attempt loaded and never recomputed, so reopening an invitation link showed "No limit" and expiry never fired. Resume is the normal path. | traced |

#### Silent failures

| Defect | Effect | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **LLM grading never ran** | `llm_auto_score` was off on every assessment, so submits never queued and the scoring cron drained an empty queue every 60 s. One answer sat pending **9 days with zero attempts** and no error anywhere. Fixed, then graded live against real Vertex spend. | live |
| **First Vertex mint failed on any new system** | The token cache used search-then-insert, which races on first creation. Invisible on an old database where the row already exists; fatal on a fresh one. **Every new deployment would have hit this.** Reproduced on a wiped database. | live |
| **Tag extraction hung forever** | It committed its "busy" state on a separate transaction, invalidating its own snapshot; the write two minutes later died on a serialization conflict and left the generator pinned on "extracting" with no error. It also raced its own cron. | live |
| **Generator screen lost its own data** | Every mutation ended with a refresh that replaced generators from the *list* route, which omits `resources`, `allowed_types` and the question count. Uploads vanished; type ticks reverted. **The server had been saving correctly the whole time.** | live |
| **Bank questions opened the wrong record** | The bank serialiser omitted `state`, so the client parsed every bank question as a draft and fetched `/drafts/<id>` — a different record on a different id sequence. Hence no options and an empty answer key. | live |
| **Scoring screen invented a queue** | An all-objective paper has no `not_needed` state at attempt level, so it sat at the default `pending` and was reported as waiting to be graded — permanently, on a perfectly healthy system. | unit |
| **Rescore ignored the grader's lock** | The cron holds an advisory lock around scoring; the HTTP route called the same method without it. Two paid Vertex calls on one candidate, two different marks, last writer wins. | live |
| **Restored database blamed the wrong thing** | Secrets are sealed with a key derived from `database.secret`, which is regenerated per database. After a restore the app reported "Vertex not configured", sending an operator to upload a key they had already uploaded. | live |
| **The contract audit under-checked** | Its Dart parser could not handle the trailing comma `dart format` writes, so it backtracked across newlines and swallowed the next method. It checked **71 call sites where there were 81**, and produced one confident false failure. | live |

#### Mistakes made during this work

Listed because they cost time and would otherwise be invisible in the diff:

- A "best-effort" error handler swallowed a Postgres error **without a savepoint**, turning a
  recoverable failure into a 500. Caught in the traceback and corrected.
- A recovery sweeper added to a cron ran unguarded at the top of the loop; one unfixable row
  would have **blocked all generation forever**. Now guarded per row.
- A scoring fix was described as preventing "one bad candidate killing the whole batch".
  **That was false** — the cron always had a per-evaluator savepoint. An agent's claim was
  repeated without checking it.
- A bad edit duplicated half of a 2,000-line screen file. Caught and repaired.
- A run command that served the wrong directory, and the app started against the wrong
  database — both cost demo time directly.

---

### Not done

> **Nobody has driven the rebuilt UI in a browser.** Everything above is verified at API and
> test level only. The generator screen was rebuilt on the last day and confirmed at route
> level. This is exactly what caused the demo failure and it is still open.

#### Parity gaps against Odoo

Roughly 86% of 42 user-triggerable operations are reachable from Flutter. Missing:

- **Question bank export** — JSON, CSV and native round-trip. The *import* half exists, so the
  app can import a payload it cannot produce.
- Bank-import CSV template download (the roster template *is* wired).
- S3 image offload.
- Queue scoring for one specific candidate — whole-assessment and single-attempt rescore both
  work.
- Tag rename, recolour and delete — merge and normalise work.
- Archive and unarchive an assessment — generators and bank questions can be.
- **Schedule dates on an assessment.** The whole stack exists and the candidate card already
  renders "Opens…", but no screen sets the value.

#### Known weaknesses

- **Accessibility: zero `Semantics` widgets in the entire app.** A candidate using a screen
  reader cannot sit an exam. That is a procurement blocker, not a nicety.
- **The proctoring simulator** drives the real violation route. It is now behind
  `--dart-define=PROCTOR_SIM=false` but **defaults to on** — build candidate bundles with it
  off.
- **No human override of an LLM mark.** A reviewer who disagrees can only re-run the same
  grader.
- Analytics and the leaderboard are computed client-side from loaded rows rather than from the
  server aggregate; they will diverge once a cohort exceeds what the console loads.
- `_finalize_sop_gen_state` documents an invariant its own caller breaks on a serialization
  failure. Flagged, not fixed — changing it changes retry semantics.
- CI has never run a test. Its pytest gate short-circuits and reports green.

install works. That exercise is what exposed the first-mint race — a bug no amount of testing
on the existing database could have found.

# Part 5 - The 2026-09-10 defect pass

Seven reported defects against the admin console, specced at
`.kiro/specs/assessment-admin-console-defects/`. This part records what changed,
why, and the evidence - so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.

**Nothing here is committed.** Both repos sit on `main`, which maps to
PRODUCTION, and the work is uncommitted in the working tree by design.
(No longer true as of 19.0.3.23.0: the pass was committed on 2026-09-11 -
backend `6c1c42966`, app `9844056` - and is part of 19.0.3.22.0, the version
prod runs.)

## 5.1 D2 / D7 - offset paging over a non-unique sort key

**The defect.** `_attempt_page()` ordered by `create_date desc` with no unique
tiebreaker. A bulk-invited cohort is created in ONE transaction, so every row
carries an identical `create_date` - `cr.now()` is the transaction timestamp.
Offset paging re-runs the query per page, and Postgres orders equal keys by
whatever the plan produces: `LIMIT n OFFSET k` is a bounded top-N heapsort while
`n + k` is below the row count and an unbounded quicksort once it is not. The
two emit ties in different orders, so a row lands on two pages while another
lands on none.

**Measured on stage:** walking `/api/v1/attempts` at limit=200 collected 2,538
rows of a stated 2,538 total - but only **2,077 distinct**. 461 attempts were
never returned. The COUNT was right and the ROWS were wrong, so every state chip
read correctly over a corrupted sample.

**Reproduced locally 2026-09-10** at stage's shape (2,539 rows, one transaction,
2 distinct `create_date` values), walking the global listing at 200/page:

| ordering | collected | distinct | lost |
|---|---|---|---|
| `create_date desc` (old) | 2,539 | 2,538 | **1** |
| `create_date desc, id desc` (new) | 2,539 | 2,539 | **0** |

**The fix.** `_NEWEST_FIRST = "create_date desc, id desc"` on every offset-paged
route (`controllers/api/admin.py`), an explicit order on the two routes that
inherited an unstated model `_order` (`forms.py`, `task_templates.py`), `name, id`
on tags and users, `date desc, id desc` on chatter, and an ordered
`servable_only` branch. `id` is the tiebreaker because it is the primary key:
unique by definition, never null, already indexed, and on a newest-first listing
it descends with the primary sort so the composite reads as one intent.

**What it does NOT fix, stated plainly.** A total order removes instability
WITHIN one walk of unchanged data. It does not make the walk a snapshot: a row
created between page 3 and page 4 still shifts every later offset. The loss is
now bounded by concurrent WRITES rather than guaranteed by the SORT.

### 5.1a The roster sort allow-list (19.0.3.22.0)

The two roster routes - `/api/v1/attempts` and
`/api/v1/assessments/<id>/candidates` - now accept `sort` and `sort_desc`, resolved
by `admin.py::_attempt_order()` through **`admin.py::_SORTABLE`**, an ALLOW-LIST of
nine UI columns, not a passthrough.

An allow-list because `search(order=...)` takes any stored field on the model:
forwarding the client's string would let a caller order the roster by
`access_token` - a bearer credential - and would 500 on a typo. It is also the
mapping itself, because three columns do not sort by the field they render:

| `sort` value | ORDER BY field | why it is not the rendered field |
|---|---|---|
| `candidate` | `candidate_name` | sorting `applicant_id` orders by the many2one's id, not the name on screen |
| `state` | `state_rank` | sorting the raw `state` key orders alphabetically, which is not the funnel order |
| `score` | **`score_percent`** | `total_score` is the OBJECTIVE sub-total only (`objective_total` is an alias of it). The SCORE cell renders `score_marks` - earned over the paper's component count, objective AND graded subjective - and the RESULT pill beside it is decided by `score_percent`. Sorting by `total_score` ordered a subjective-heavy paper by its MCQ section alone, so "16 / 20" sat below "5 / 20" under a descending caret. It is also the only normalised key here: the denominator varies per drawn paper, so a bare numerator cannot rank across candidates |

The other six - `invite`, `answered`, `result`, `released`, `remarks`, `flag` - map
to `invite_state`, `answered_count`, `result`, `results_released`, `manual_remark`,
`manual_flagged`.

**Every branch ends in `id`, in the same direction as the column.** These columns tie
far worse than `create_date` did: `results_released` and `manual_flagged` are
booleans, so sorting a 711-row cohort by FLAG puts ~700 rows on one key, and
`manual_remark` is empty on nearly all of them. Without the tiebreaker §5.1 is not an
edge case a big cohort might hit - it is every page of every sort.

**An unknown or absent `sort` is not an error.** It degrades to `_NEWEST_FIRST`, so a
client one deploy behind, or one remembering a renamed column, gets the roster it
always got. `candidate_name` (stored related on `applicant_id.partner_name`) and
`state_rank` (stored compute on `state`) are the two stored columns this adds to
`assessments_be_evaluator`; both backfill on `-u` with no migration script, and
skipping `-u` leaves them absent and answers a 500 the first time a header is clicked.

## 5.2 D2 - search that reaches the whole population

Five of eleven admin search boxes were already server-backed. The reported
"only works for 400 entries" was exactly one screen: **Responses** walked
`/api/v1/responses` at `maxPages: 2` (400 of 31,462 rows measured on stage) and
filtered in memory, and the route accepted no search term at all.

- `assessments.be.response._be_search_domain()` - the shared predicate over
  assessment, candidate and question, the same three axes Odoo's own response
  search view offers. Owned by the model so the route and the view cannot drift.
- The Responses box is now **hybrid**: the term goes to the server for those
  three axes AND the local pass still runs over the cache. Sending it to the
  server INSTEAD would have broken answer-text search outright - that text is
  rendered and REDACTED client-side, and a second copy of the redaction rules on
  the server is the duplication that caused the original defect.
- The Ledger pages server-side instead of slicing a 1,000-row walk.
- Task templates walk their pages instead of stopping at the 200-row clamp.
- The per-assessment Leaderboard tab reads its own cohort rather than the
  console-wide `attempts` cache, whose 25-page cap is shared across every
  assessment.
- `test/assessment/every_search_box_declares_its_scope_test.dart` is the
  register: every box is `server`, `local` with a stated reason, or `hybrid`.

## 5.3 D1 - the manual flag and the internal remark

**THE DESIGN REVERSED ONCE, and the reversal is worth reading before you touch
this.** The first pass put the flag on the PERSON (`hr.applicant`), so a concern
raised on one assessment followed the candidate to every other one they sat.
CJ rejected that on 2026-09-10: a flag is a statement about ONE SITTING, not
about a human being. It now lives on `assessments.be.evaluator`.

If you are tempted to move it back to the person, the argument that lost was
"the Leaderboard is grouped by applicant so it has no attempt row" - which is
false for the per-assessment Leaderboard TAB, the only leaderboard that shows a
flag. The cross-assessment dashboard panel deliberately shows none, because a
person who was flagged on one of six assessments is not "a flagged person".

**Flag and remark are INDEPENDENT features.** This is the second thing that
changed. The flag is a pure toggle with NO reason text - click to raise, click
again to clear, wherever it is shown. The remark is free text that can exist
with or without a flag, and a flag can exist with no remark. Neither implies
the other.

| field | model | why |
|---|---|---|
| `manual_flagged` | `assessments.be.evaluator` | indexed; the thing filtered on |
| `manual_flagged_by_id`, `manual_flagged_at` | `assessments.be.evaluator` | readonly, stamped by the route; they describe the FLAG, never the remark |
| `manual_remark` | `assessments.be.evaluator` | independent free text; refused past 5,000 chars, never truncated |

`POST /api/v1/attempts/<evaluator_id>/flag`, `@require_manager` (the Admin rung;
`require_operator` is the read-only Manager and stays refused). Body carries
`flagged` and/or `remark`, **and only the keys PRESENT are changed** - that is
what makes the two independent on the wire, and it is asserted against the
request body rather than the resulting state, because a client that helpfully
sent `remark: ''` alongside a toggle would wipe a remark nobody asked it to
touch.

**Where it appears.** The flag is one shared widget (`FlagToggle`) on every
surface - an outline flag when clear, filled red when raised, tooltip
"Raised by Akshay Kumar on Sep 8th, 2026" built once in
`CandidateFlag.raisedSentence` so three surfaces cannot word it differently:

- the **Candidates** table, as the last column, with a **Remarks** column
  immediately before it;
- the **Leaderboard** table, as the last column (no "Flagged" word-badge - the
  icon IS the statement);
- the **attempt header**, beside the candidate's name. The remark renders as its
  own section BELOW the violations/outlier/integrity notices, and only when a
  remark exists. It does not displace or reword those notices - an earlier
  version rendered a large banner in their place, which is what CJ rejected.

**Two edge cases that were wrong on the first pass and are now pinned:**

1. `str_arg(max_len=...)` truncates SILENTLY. Right for a search term, wrong for
   a remark - the operator would be told it saved while the end of their
   reasoning was dropped. The route refuses past the bound instead.
2. `bool("false")` is `True`. A JSON client that stringifies booleans would have
   RAISED a flag on the exact request that meant to withdraw one. Presence is
   checked against the raw body (so a missing key cannot read as "clear"), and
   the value goes through `bool_arg`.

A third, found by the client tests: `CandidateFlag.fromJson` short-circuited on
`flagged` being false, which silently dropped every remark left on an unflagged
attempt. Independence has to be honoured in the PARSER too, not only in the
route.

**The disclosure contract (C3).** The flag and the remark go in
`evaluator_admin_row` - `flags.manual_flagged` plus a `candidate_flag` block -
and nowhere else. They are on **`applicant_brief` never**: that brief is shared
and nested inside candidate payloads, and is the only realistic leak path.
`leaderboard_row` carries none either, for the design reason above.
`tests/test_api_invariants.py::TestNothingInternalReachesACandidate` walks every
candidate-facing serializer RECURSIVELY for any flag key at any depth, has a
counterexample test proving the walker catches a planted key, and a vacuity
guard proving the fixture actually flags people.

**Results CSV.** The results export carries `Flagged` (`yes` when flagged, EMPTY
otherwise - never "no") and `Flag Remarks` (the remark, or empty).

Four time-analysis columns are appended AFTER those two, in this order (appending
is the only safe widening for a spreadsheet keyed to column position), computed by
`services/pace.py` and the median read once per file:
`submitted_at` (written like `started_at`, empty when unset), `time_taken_minutes`
(one decimal, empty when either end is missing or the span is not positive),
`test_median_minutes` (one decimal, the same on every row, empty when no sitting
qualifies) and `pace` (`Fast` / `Normal` / `Slow`, empty without a time or a
median). The pace ratio is taken / median seconds, rounded half up to 2 decimals
in Decimal: `<= 0.75` Fast, `>= 1.25` Slow, else Normal
(`PACE_FAST_AT_OR_BELOW` / `PACE_SLOW_AT_OR_ABOVE` in `constants.py`, twins of the
client's `kPaceFastAtOrBelow` / `kPaceSlowAtOrAbove`).

Three roster columns are appended AFTER the time block, in this order:
`invite_state` (the raw value `none` / `queued` / `sent` / `failed`, like
`candidate_state`; `none` when unset), `answered_count` (the stored count, 0 when
unset) and `question_count` (the size of THAT candidate's own paper:
`evaluator.total_questions`, the stored count of the frozen `question_order`, the
same figure the admin candidate serializers send as `total_questions` beside
Answered; 0 for a candidate with no frozen paper). Two integer columns on purpose:
"8 / 14" in one cell is read as a date by spreadsheets. All three are stored
columns on the evaluator, so they ride the row prefetch (no query per candidate).
The full header is now 30 columns: the 23 base columns (through `Flag Remarks`),
the four time columns, then these three. **The Results export is now the one
per-candidate file**: it replaces the app's old browser-built "Export Roster" CSV
(Candidate, Email, State, Invite, Answered, Score, Result, Released), whose every
field it now carries; the Responses export stays one row per answer and gets no
roster columns.

**A sitting's span is capped at its deadline.** It runs from `started_at` to the
EARLIER of `submitted_at` and `deadline_datetime` (to `submitted_at` when there is
no deadline), and only a positive span counts (`pace.span_seconds`, the one place
the rule lives, so the median, `time_taken_minutes` and `pace` agree). Why:
`submitted_at` is stamped when a sitting is SETTLED (`write` to `submitted`), not
when it ended, so an expired paper settled later by the cron or on the candidate's
next visit is stamped after the deadline it ended on. On a local clone 7 of 60
timed sittings read longer than their limit, the worst by 9,014 s, which inflated
"time taken", dragged the median and tagged people Slow for a delay that was not
theirs. The export's `submitted_at` cell stays the raw stamp. The client applies
the same rule. `deadline_datetime` is a stored compute from the paper's CURRENT
duration, so editing a paper's duration afterwards moves the cap, the median and
the pace of past sittings.

`manual_flagged_only` is its OWN filter parameter. `flagged_only` still means
exactly the three AUTOMATIC advisory flags (`integrity_alert`, `score_outlier`,
`scoring_error_flag`) - folding the manual flag into that OR-chain would have
silently changed what every existing review-queue call returns.

## 5.4 D6 - the Decided Outcomes donut at 4+ digits

The requested remedy - `FittedBox(fit: BoxFit.scaleDown)` - had been in the
widget since SNo 163, so the question was never "does it scale" but "what does
it scale TO". Measured in Chrome against the real DM Mono / Plus Jakarta Sans
faces, because `flutter_test` forces the Ahem face and reports a different
scale:

| centre value | natural | scale | ratio px | LABEL px |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `13/19` | 79.7 | 1.000 | 30.0 | 11.0 |
| `396/572` | 113.4 | 0.817 | 24.5 | 9.0 |
| `1466/2538` | 147.1 | 0.630 | 18.9 | **6.9** |
| `12345/67890` | 180.8 | 0.512 | 15.4 | **5.6** |

**The cause was the converse of the hypothesis table's H2.** H2 asked whether
the LABEL drives the RATIO's scale - it does not. The defect is the ratio
driving the LABEL's: one shared `FittedBox` scales to whichever child overflows
most, which past three digits is always the ratio, so `PASSED` was dragged to
5.6px. The fix is one `FittedBox` per child; the label measures ~42px against a
92.6px bound, so its own scale is 1.000 at every figure.

Ruled out with evidence: `DonutChart` has exactly one caller and it passes no
`size`; the hosting `Row` throws no overflow at 460px; Odoo's `.etp-donut`
renders no number inside the ring at all (the hole shows the static word
"Results"), so H3 was structurally impossible; and `ScoreRing` in the
neighbouring card measures 42.1px into an 86px hole - it looks unguarded but
does not overflow at any digit count this platform produces.

## 5.5 D5 - names readable in full

`GridLink.maxLines` defaults to 2 with a tooltip; the three fixed-`rowHeight`
dashboard grids opt back to 1 explicitly, because a fixed-height row CLIPS
rather than growing. On the Odoo side `backend.scss` unwraps only the name
columns of two named lists, scoped with `:has()` on a header column each view
alone carries, with a 200px floor - an auto-layout table sizes a column from its
MIN-CONTENT width, so a cell allowed to wrap COLLAPSES, and without the floor a
40px row became 269px.

## 5.6 D4 - the JSON import template

`services/bank_json_template.py` renders both flavours, the two wizard buttons,
`GET /api/v1/bank/template/json` and the schema section of this knowledge base
from ONE set of definitions - see 4.1. (Changed in 19.0.3.23.0: the two wizard
buttons are now one **Download Template** control with a Template choice - CSV,
JSON (harness), JSON (native bank export) - dispatched by
`action_download_selected_template`; both flavours still come from
`bank_json_template.py`. W9, ETP_PLANS_AND_STRATEGY.md Part 4 §4.4.)

## 5.7 D3 - Odoo / Flutter parity

**All twelve `absent` + `blocking` rows are closed.** The cohort-wide re-score of
failed attempts (the method existed on no view; its in-memory `filtered()` over
the whole cohort became an indexed `search()` domain), four task-template rows,
four Studio-form rows, and finally the three graphical editors: the labelling
annotation editor, the Form Studio item editor and its media upload.

The rule that mattered on all three of the last ones is that **the editor owns
no rules**. Each writes through the model method the API already calls -
`apply_studio_annotation_item`, `validate_structure()` / `form_item_kinds()`,
and the existing `/api/v1/forms/media` routes - so a form the back office
accepts is exactly a form publish accepts, and the SSRF allow-list on media
lives in one place. An editor with its own copy of the rules is how a record
becomes valid on one screen and refused on the other.

Changed in 19.0.3.23.0 (ETP_PLANS_AND_STRATEGY.md Part 4 §4.5-§4.6):
- The Form Studio form, and the item editor on it, are **read-only in Odoo**
  (`edit="0"`, `readonly="1"` on `structure_json`): the Flutter designer
  re-saves an open form every 0.9 s, so an Odoo edit was silently overwritten.
  **Publish** (was "Send to Candidates") stays, and can be pressed again: each
  press makes a new draft assessment. The editor now authors task-template
  structure in Odoo instead, with the publish check skipped
  (`skip_publish_check`), because a template is never published and its answer
  keys are optional.
- Retry Failed Scoring (the cohort-wide re-score above) now also refuses a
  cancelled paper and a paper whose Kill is still stopping (S5, S1).

See 4.2 for the row-by-row inventory and the two recorded limits (`box_px`
markers are pixels and deliberately not redrawn; a marker with neither geometry
nor a label cannot be repaired in the editor).

### The data-loss defect the review caught, and the guard that closes it

**Found by opening the annotation editor on a real question rather than by
running its tests.** Question 1417 on a production-shaped database carries 46
markers and 349 keyed labels, and ALL of its geometry is stored as `box_px` -
the DOM-capture lane's pixels, which the model deliberately refuses to hand out
as drawable regions. `as_studio_annotation_item` can only express a marker it
can draw or key, so the editor opened with 9 of the 46.

Pressing Save then sent back what the editor was holding, and
`apply_studio_annotation_item` applied it faithfully:

    BEFORE   label_boxes=46  detections=46  ideal_labels=349
    sends    regions=0  golden=9  count=9
    refusals []                      <- the server raised no objection
    AFTER    label_boxes=9   detections=9   ideal_labels=9

Thirty-seven markers and 340 label entries deleted off a paper candidates had
already sat, in one click, with an empty refusal list. The widget did warn on
screen - but a warning is advisory, the operator is mid-correction, and nothing
stopped it.

**The guard is on the SERVER**, so it protects the API route as well as the
widget: a save is refused when it would shrink the marker set AND some of the
markers were never openable in the editor. The distinction matters both ways -
deleting a box you drew is an ordinary edit and must still work, so the guard
fires only on the markers the editor was never shown. `allow_marker_drop` is the
explicit escape hatch for a caller that genuinely means to shorten the paper;
the editor never sends it, which is what stops it happening by accident.

The first version of the guard refused EVERY reduction and broke three existing
tests, all of which legitimately delete a marker. That failure is the reason the
rule is written as "was it hidden from the editor" rather than "did the count go
down".

## 5.9 The contract audit learned to follow an alias

`tools/verify.sh --quick` runs `tools/contract_audit.py`, which compares the
keys the Flutter client SENDS against the keys each route READS. It recognises
`body().get("x")` and `kw.get("x")`, but it matched on the receiver's NAME
against a fixed list - so a route that did `raw = body()` and then
`raw.get("remark")` looked like it ignored the key.

That is not a hypothetical cost. The audit reported
`/api/v1/attempts/*/flag  client sends but server IGNORES: ['remark']`, a
reviewer believed it, and time went into chasing a bug that did not exist - the
route honours `remark` and always did, which a live call confirmed in seconds.

Two changes, because either alone leaves the trap set: the local is now called
`payload` (a name the audit knows), and `_index_function` collects locals bound
to a payload call so `x = body()` followed by `x.get("k")` counts as a read. A
checker that cries wolf is worse than no checker, because the next real finding
is the one nobody acts on.

## 5.8 Deploying this

**A version bump alone does not apply any of it.** Odoo marks a module
`to upgrade` only from the `-u` flag (`odoo/modules/loading.py`); `update_list()`
counts a newer manifest version but does not schedule the upgrade. The deploy
must run `-u assessments_be_v2`. This still holds for 19.0.3.23.0; its order
(backend first, one `-u` job before new pods take traffic, never in the
Dockerfile CMD) is in ETP_PLANS_AND_STRATEGY.md Part 0 §0.5.

Verified locally on a copy of the dev database, migrating `19.0.3.14.0` ->
`19.0.3.19.0` with these changes: **4.4 seconds, exit 0**, all migration scripts
ran, indexes built `CONCURRENTLY`, 47 evaluators and 169 responses intact, and
the new views and menus registered.

**No data migration is needed for the flag.** The four `manual_*` columns are
added to `assessments_be_evaluator` by the ORM on upgrade and are NULL on every
row that predates them, which is safe: Odoo reads a NULL boolean as `False`, and
`("manual_flagged", "=", False)` matches NULL rows - so the unflagged filter
returns the whole cohort rather than only the rows written since.

Note for anyone reading an older checkout: an earlier pass created five
`be_flag*` columns on `hr_applicant` and a stored related `candidate_flagged` on
the evaluator. That design was reversed before anything shipped. The columns may
still exist in a local development database that was upgraded mid-pass; they are
unused, carry no data anybody entered through the shipped UI, and can be dropped
at leisure. Nothing in the module reads them.
